title: How to Read and Apply Old Testament Law
subtitle: A clear guide to reading the law of Moses as a Christian, understanding the moral, civil, and ceremonial categories, and applying the Old Testament commands today without legalism or neglect

sections.title: The Chapters We Skip
sections.body:
Be honest about what happens when your reading plan reaches Leviticus. You slow down, then you stop, then you skip ahead to a Psalm. The laws about mildew and goats and torn garments feel like a foreign country with no road back to your life.

So we ignore them. And then we are baffled when a skeptic asks why we eat shellfish but quote Leviticus on other matters.

The law is not a problem to be managed. It is the word of God, more than six hundred commands given to a redeemed people, and Jesus said he did not come to abolish it. If we cannot say how the law applies to us, we have a hole in the center of our Bible, and we have handed our critics an easy weapon. This is the work of learning to read the law as Christians: neither dragging every rule into the present as binding, nor throwing the whole of it away as irrelevant. Both are failures of nerve. The text deserves better.

sections.title: The Law Comes After the Rescue
sections.body:
The most important fact about the law is where it sits. It does not come first. It comes after the exodus, after God has already rescued Israel from Egypt by his own arm. He saves them, and then he gives them the law, and the order is everything.

The law was never a ladder to climb into God's favor. It was the shape of life for a people already loved.

Get this backward and you turn the Old Testament into a religion of earning, which it never was. The Ten Commandments open by reminding Israel who brought them out of slavery, and only then issue the commands. Grace first. Obedience as the response to grace. This is the same gospel logic that runs through the whole Bible. Read the law as the household rules of a family already adopted, not the entrance exam of a people trying to get in, and the whole thing changes color.

sections.title: Moral, Civil, and Ceremonial
sections.body:
The old teachers divided the law into three kinds, and the distinction, while not perfect, still helps. There is moral law, which reflects the unchanging character of God, like the commands against murder and idolatry. There is civil law, which governed Israel as a nation in its land. And there is ceremonial law, which regulated sacrifice, priesthood, and ritual cleanness.

These categories are not stamped on the text in colored ink. They are a tool for asking the right question of each command.

The moral law endures because God's character does not change. The civil law expressed that morality for a particular nation that no longer exists as a theocracy, so its principles carry forward while its specific penalties do not. The ceremonial law pointed forward to Christ and has reached its goal in him, which is why we no longer sacrifice lambs. The book of Hebrews is one long argument that the shadows have met their substance. Use the three categories as a question, not a label. Ask what kind of command this is, and you will know how it reaches you.

sections.title: Every Law Runs to Christ
sections.body:
There is a deeper unity beneath the three categories, and it is a person. Jesus said the law and the prophets were about him. He is the true temple, the final sacrifice, the spotless lamb, the great high priest, the obedient Israel who kept the law we broke.

This means you have not finished reading any law until you have asked how it points to Christ.

The sacrifices teach you the cost of sin and the necessity of substitution, and then they send you to the cross where the real payment was made. The cleanness laws teach you that a holy God cannot be approached casually, and then they send you to the one who makes the unclean clean with a word. The civil laws show you the justice and mercy of God's character, fulfilled in the King who rules in righteousness. Read every command as a signpost, and the law stops being a museum of dead rules. It becomes a long finger pointing at the Son.

sections.title: How a Single Law Reaches Today
sections.body:
So how do you actually apply a specific ancient law. You ask what it reveals about God and about what he requires of his people, and you carry that principle across the bridge into your own life under the new covenant.

Take the command to build a parapet around your roof so no one falls and dies. You do not have a flat roof or a covenant obligation to Israel.

But the law reveals a God who cares about your neighbor's safety and holds you responsible for the dangers on your property. So you fence your pool. You salt your icy steps. The specific command was for them. The character of God behind it is for everyone, always. This is the move that keeps you from both errors. You honor the law as God's word by listening for what it teaches about him, and you apply that with wisdom, rather than reenacting iron age agriculture or pretending the text says nothing at all.

sections.title: Love Was the Point
sections.body:
When Jesus was asked to name the greatest commandment, he reached into the law and pulled out two threads: love God with everything, love your neighbor as yourself. On these, he said, hang all the rest. Every command in those six hundred was an attempt to spell out what love looks like in a real life with real neighbors.

The law was never an end in itself. It was love, written down for people who needed it written down.

We still need it written down. Left to ourselves we will call our preferences holiness and our neglect freedom. The law remains a gift, a mirror that shows us our sin, a tutor that drives us to Christ, and a guide that shows the redeemed how to live. Do not skip it. Read it on your knees, looking for the God who saved a people and then taught them to love. Then go and do the same.
